title: Shabari
hook: an old woman of the forest who waited years for one visit

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kabandha rose from the fire and pointed the way. Find Sugriva, visit Shabari.

On the western shore of Lake Pampa there's a hermitage that has outlived its teachers. The sages who lived there, disciples of the great rishi Matanga, have all left this world. One person stayed behind: an old woman, an ascetic, living alone among the trees. Before they went, her teachers told her that Rama would come one day, and that she should wait for him. She has been waiting a long time.
screen: `A HERMITAGE BY LAKE PAMPA.` → `THE TEACHERS ARE GONE.` → `ONE WOMAN WAITS.`

segments.voice: Her name is Shabari. Valmiki calls her a shramani, a woman ascetic, and some readers hear in her name the Shabaras, a forest people. When the brothers arrive, she rises, bows at their feet, and welcomes them the way the old texts describe: water for their feet, water to rinse the mouth, a seat. Rama asks what you'd ask any respected elder. Has your practice gone well? Have you mastered anger? Are your vows kept? Is your mind at peace? She answers, in effect: today my practice has borne fruit, because I've seen you. She has gathered forest fruits for him, and she offers them. Look at who is honoring whom. Rama is a prince of Ayodhya. Shabari is an old woman living alone in the forest, with no rank at all. The text makes no speech about it. It just shows a prince sitting in her hermitage, asking about her inner life, and receiving what she gives. Then there's the story told in many homes: Shabari tasted each berry first, so only the sweet ones went to Rama, and he ate them gladly. It isn't in Valmiki. It grew in later tellings, in regional Ramayanas, songs and sermons. In Valmiki she simply offers the fruits she gathered. Both are worth knowing: what the old text says, and what later devotion added.
screen: `SHABARI, A WOMAN ASCETIC.` · `MY PRACTICE HAS BORNE FRUIT.` · `A PRINCE IN A FOREST HERMITAGE.` · `THE TASTED BERRIES: A LATER TELLING.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who has waited a long time for something good; maybe it's you. Breathe in and feel the waiting, steady rather than impatient; breathe out and let it be enough to keep the place ready, the way Shabari kept the hermitage. You don't need to know when; just sit, ready.
Shabari. The forest ascetic who waited at Matanga's hermitage, and said her practice bore fruit the day Rama came.
Your line: my practice has borne fruit. Tomorrow, more time with Shabari. That's day five hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Shabari is honored as a model of devotion (bhakti) that needs no rank or learning; the berry story is told in later Ramayanas, songs and sermons, and some temples and festivals honor her.

original.note: Sanskrit śabarī: the name of the ascetic at Matanga's hermitage, which some readers link to the Śabara, a forest people.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shabari is the woman who tasted the berries.
what it means: in Valmiki she's an ascetic whose long practice is fulfilled by Rama's visit.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 74 calls her a śramaṇī and has her offer gathered fruits; the tasted-berry motif appears in later regional and devotional retellings.

chat.says: What happens when Rama finally reaches Shabari?
options: She welcomes him as an honored guest, offers forest fruit, and says her practice has borne fruit.
She tells him where Ravana has hidden Sita, then sends him across the sea to Lanka.
She asks him to lift a curse from her teachers, who were turned into trees by a sage.
chat.meaning: Shabari greets Rama with water, a seat and the fruit she gathered, and says seeing him is the fruit of her practice.

Shabari.meaning: the old woman ascetic at Matanga's hermitage

Matanga.meaning: the rishi whose disciples taught Shabari

Ayodhya.meaning: Rama's home city, his father's capital

recall: a forest giant no weapon could kill

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 73–74 (Matanga's hermitage; Shabari welcomes Rama)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering and differ between editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper uses.
'Her name points to the Shabaras, a forest people': standard reading of the name; Valmiki does not dwell on her birth. Confirm wording.
'A community many in his world would have looked down on': interpretive; a Keeper may wish to soften.

The tasted-berry story: attributed here only to 'later tellings'. A Keeper may want to name specific sources (it is popular in north Indian devotional tradition; its exact earliest source is debated).
